title: Revit AI Automation Pricing: Plan the Demo and the Budget
summary: Prepare a Revit AI software demo and budget for seats, usage, setup, and review time, with a practical cost-per-accepted-deliverable example.
body_markdown:
Putting a number on Revit AI automation is harder than it looks. One tool lists a monthly price, another is sold by quote, and Autodesk now ships an assistant inside Revit itself. The pricing page also leaves out the two things that usually decide what you really spend: how the product meters usage, and how much of your team's time goes into checking and fixing what it produces. A demo is the best place to find out both, as long as you bring the right file and the right task.


## Revit AI automation software pricing demo


Here is what public pricing looks like as of November 13, 2026.


The[ArchiLabs pricing page](https://archilabs.ai/pricing) lists Desktop from $19 per month plus usage credits. The subscription gives you the product, and usage credits cover the work the agent does, so how much your team asks of it shapes the monthly total. Desktop runs on Windows, edits native models in Revit 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027, and also works with AutoCAD files.


BIMLOGIQ offers Argus through a demo and installation process on its[product page](https://bimlogiq.com/) , and you get the price as a quote. Ask for one that names your seats and billing term and carries a date, because terms change.


Autodesk's Revit Assistant is built into Revit 2027 and later. It answers help questions, and it can also query and modify the model. Autodesk's[notes on Revit 2027.3 and 2027.4](https://www.autodesk.com/blogs/aec/2026/11/10/whats-new-in-revit-2027-3-and-2027-4/) describe schedule and graphics operations and traceability for the changes it makes. If your office is on Revit 2023 through 2026, you can't use it, because it isn't available in those releases. If you're on 2027, check how your Autodesk licensing covers it before you assume it's free or an extra cost.


## What actually drives the bill


Usage units deserve the most attention. A credit, a message and a run are different units, and a price per unit tells you little until you know how many units a real task uses. Ask the vendor what a long job costs, such as filling room parameters across a whole building, and what happens when a task fails partway through and has to be run again. Two plans with similar headline prices can end up far apart once retries and large models come into it.


Seats come next. A tool that one BIM specialist uses every day costs something different from one that dozens of project architects open now and then, and per-seat rules can suit one of those patterns better than the other.


Some products connect Revit to an outside AI client through MCP or a similar connector. When that's the setup, the AI client may need its own subscription with its own usage limits. That cost isn't part of the Revit tool's price, and it's easy to miss.


Then there's the cost that never shows up on an invoice: the time someone spends checking what the tool changed and fixing what it got wrong. Review time decides whether automation pays off. A cheap tool whose every result has to be rechecked line by line can cost more than a pricier one whose output your team can accept after a quick look.


## Bring your own file to the demo


A demo on the vendor's own model shows the product at its best. To find out what it will cost you, bring a Revit file from your current release and a task your team actually repeats. A room-data update from an approved spreadsheet works well. It's common and tedious, and it's easy to check, because you already know which rooms should change and what they should change to.


Add a couple of rows to the spreadsheet that shouldn't match anything, such as a room number that isn't in the model and one that appears twice. See what the tool does with them. Does it skip them and tell you, or does it guess? That tells you how much review the workflow will need.


Then change a few values in the spreadsheet and ask for the update again. Projects get revised all the time, so the cost of the second run and the tenth run matters more than one clean first run. Watch whether the setup carries over and whether the rerun changes only what you changed.


## Comparing against doing it by hand


Once you've seen the task done, compare the cost per accepted result with the manual version of the same job. Count review and correction on both sides. People check manual room-data updates too. If you charge the AI for review but treat manual work as error-free, the comparison is skewed one way, and if you leave out the AI's review time, it's skewed the other. Our guide to[measuring Revit automation net savings](https://archilabs.ai/posts/measure-revit-automation-net-savings) covers preparation, execution and review in more detail.


If you'd like to try this with ArchiLabs, bring your file, your Revit release and your spreadsheet to a[Desktop walkthrough](https://archilabs.ai/desktop) . Desktop works directly in native Revit models from 2023 through 2027, so you can watch the update happen in your own project and price it against work you already know well.
